newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Funds flee Asia but heavy in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Funds flee Asia but heavy in Hong Kong.

text.p: Funds are fleeing most parts of Asia in favour of better performing markets elsewhere, but they have maintained overweight positions in Hong Kong.

However, that was not necessarily an overwhelming vote of confidence in the territory. Experts said the overweight position has been reduced substantially in the past three weeks, and should be viewed as a comment that the rest of the region offered poor value.
"They can't go underweight because the rest of the region is diabolically positioned at the moment," one head trader said.
International funds have cut their Asian weightings and were holding all of it in Hong Kong, reducing Asian-dedicated allocations from heavily overweight to overweight.

Asian funds were scrambling to find some alternative to Hong Kong after a disastrous foray into Malaysia just before the government announcement of new lending restrictions helped to depress Malaysian stocks by 14 percent, said David Semple, strategist at Peregrine Investment Management.

A recent survey of 61 Asian funds revealed an aggregate Hong Kong position of 35.4 percent at the end of February, down from 40.4 percent at the end of 1996 and compared to a 28-percent benchmark in the Morgan Stanley Capital Index, Semple said.
"They're taking money out, and my impression is that has happened in March," he said. "But they're still overweight."
However, the U.S. investment bank Merrill Lynch seemed to buck the general trend on Friday, saying it was moving funds into Indian stock markets from Latin America.
Merrill said in a strategy report: "India appears to offer some of the best value regionally." It said Korea and Thailand had been major regional commitments in its portfolio strategy.

The experts said Hong Kong continued to offer a complicated picture. Blue chips were slumping, red chips -- companies heavily exposed to China -- were soaring, volume was strong, institutional money was leaving, but funds were overweight.
They said the situation reflected both the extent of the negative sentiment towards most of Asia and a developing quirk in the Hong Kong market.

The prospect of higher U.S. interest rates sent jitters throughout most markets around the world, but Asia -- and Hong Kong blue chips -- suffered the worst damage thanks to a disappointing economic performance so far this year.

"People are taking the view that the economic outlook for Asia in 1997 will continue to be dull, particularly the outlook for exports," Semple said. "It looks as though the downturn will be prolonged. People were looking for a bounce-back in 1997, but now it looks like it'll be 1998."

The Hang Seng index of blue-chip stocks has fallen from an all-time closing high of 13,868.24 on January 20 to a 1997 low of 12,055.17 on April 3. The index has since regained some ground, closing 81.07 points weaker at 12,645.76 on Friday.

Meanwhile, the red chips were climbing, boosting volume and creating a two-tiered market where stocks were being tugged in opposite directions by interest rate policies in the U.S. and China. Chinese rates were expected to fall later this year.
"The only thing anyone's buying is anything with red in it, or anything in China," the head trader said.
Red chips were trading at 25-times 1997 earnings compared to 12-times for the blue chips, said Tina So, assistant director at Schroders Investment Management.
"They are extremely richly priced," she said.
So saw a bottom of 12,000 for the index with the direction of U.S. interest rates likely to be clarified at the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee meeting next month.
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6470
